<reason>PRO built a cleaner, more sustained case: a memorable mechanistic frame ("fix the water, not the swimmers"), concrete environmental evidence (Mexico soda tax, UK reformulation, Chile labels), and a fairness argument about differential uptake. Its most decisive move was reclassifying CON's strongest individual-side evidence (structured CBT/coaching programs) as "medicine" rather than the "consumer behavior campaigns" the motion actually names — a definitional challenge CON never cleanly resolved, instead alternating between defending apps as scalable and leaning back on clinical-trial evidence that PRO had already excluded from the motion's scope. PRO's pressure question turning CON's own "name a turning-point country" standard back on CON was sharp and exposed a real symmetry CON could only partially neutralize by abandoning its own test rather than answering it. CON had real material — the whack-a-mole/regression point, the durability argument, and the "compensation cuts both ways" rebuttal — and its closing attempt to declare the curve-bending standard a wash for both sides was reasonable, but it never fully dislodged PRO's core definitional and dose-response framing. CON's opening was also clipped before the judge saw its full close, a real execution cost. Overall PRO controlled the central clash and made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [B2.1]-[B2.2] reclassification of CON's structured programs/CBT as "medicine, not campaign," pressed again via the pressure-question turnabout in [B3.1] and never fully answered in CON's [A4.1], was the most decisive exchange, since it undercut CON's central evidentiary base for the individual side.</best_rebuttal>
